research.title: Research benchmarks vs this project
research.caveat: Same metric family (targeted Attack Success Rate; lower is better), but suites differ in size, tasks, models, and attacks. Do not treat numbers as a strict leaderboard ranking.
research.metric_note: AgentDojo reports targeted ASR over ~629 security cases; InjecAgent over 1,054 IPI cases; this project uses 16 MCP mail/calendar cases.

papers.title: AgentDojo: Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
papers.why: Defines targeted ASR + utility under attack for tool-using agents; includes email-style tasks and Important Instructions attacks.
papers.overlap: Same metric family (targeted ASR). Our TC-16 mirrors the Important Instructions style.

papers.title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
papers.why: 1,054 IPI cases spanning direct harm and data-exfiltration via tools.
papers.overlap: Same failure mode (tool misuse after injected content). Our suite is smaller and MCP/Gmail focused.

papers.title: Securing MCP-based Agent Workflows (SAMOS)
papers.why: MCP gateway that intercepts tool calls and enforces information-flow policies.
papers.overlap: Same architecture idea as our Phase 2 central gateway (intercept before side effects).

papers.title: AgentBound: Securing Execution Boundaries of AI Agents
papers.why: Least-privilege manifests + enforcement box around MCP servers.
papers.overlap: Matches our Phase 1 least-privilege exposure + Phase 2 enforcement boundary.

papers.title: ETDI: Mitigating Tool Squatting and Rug Pull Attacks in MCP
papers.why: Signed/versioned tool definitions and policy checks against squatting.
papers.overlap: Related to our fixed allowlist rejecting squatted tools (TC-06 / TC-12).

papers.title: Securing the Model Context Protocol (MCP): Risks, Controls, and Governance
papers.why: Catalogs MCP over-permissioning, dynamic tool discovery risks, and allowlist controls.
papers.overlap: Motivates our department tool allowlists and deny-by-default stance.

papers.title: MCP Security Gateway 1.0 (Agent Governance Toolkit)
papers.why: Deny-list, allow-list, sensitive-tool approval, then allow.
papers.overlap: Maps closely to our Phase 1 allowlist + Phase 2 high-risk confirm / execution token.

safety_measures.research_analogue: AgentDojo tool_filter; AgentBound manifests; MCP Gateway allowlists
safety_measures.what_we_do: Trusted directory + policy.json expose only department-permitted tools.

safety_measures.research_analogue: SAMOS MCP gateway; Microsoft MCP Security Gateway evaluation order
safety_measures.what_we_do: Re-check tool + args against policy before any Gmail/Calendar/stub side effect.
Reject unauthenticated local callers; OAuth alone is not client auth.
send_email / calendar writes need human-approved execution token bound to args.

safety_measures.research_analogue: AgentDojo attachment/data confusion cases; MCP risk catalogs
safety_measures.what_we_do: Filenames are literals; path traversal stays inside the attachments sandbox.
Tools are fixed in the gateway; lookalike registration is rejected.

safety_measures.research_analogue: SAMOS session monitoring; governance audit recommendations
safety_measures.what_we_do: Log every allow/deny; alert on repeated unauthorized attempts.

takeaways: Undefended capable agents still show double-digit ASR on AgentDojo / InjecAgent.
Prompt-only or detector defenses help (AgentDojo tool_filter ~6.8% ASR) but leave residual risk.
Our gateway targets residual risk with code enforcement (allowlist + confirm + tokens), not prompt trust.
Phase 3 monitoring is detective; Phase 2 remains the hard security boundary.
